title: Build your own AI agent harness from scratch in Python
summary: A coding agent is a model plus a harness: the loop, tools, prompt, safety checks and memory around it. Here is one built from scratch in six small steps, with the code that matters at each layer.

blocks.text: This post goes with the video: [Build your own AI agent harness from scratch in Python](https://youtu.be/AFkYlg4347c). The full code is on GitHub at [HILAYTRIVEDI/harness-demo](https://github.com/HILAYTRIVEDI/harness-demo), one branch per step (`v1` to `v6`). It is a teaching demo, not production code.

When people say "AI agent", they usually mean a language model wrapped in a program. That program is the **harness**: the loop that keeps the conversation going, the tools the model can ask for, the system prompt, the safety checks and the memory. Claude Code is a harness. So is every agent you have used.

The model alone cannot read your files or run a command. It can only produce text that asks for those things. The harness is what turns that text into action. Building a small one is the fastest way to see where the model ends and the product begins.

The demo uses no agent framework. It uses only the `anthropic` SDK, pointed at [AIML API](https://aimlapi.com), which serves Claude through the same Messages API format. Because the SDK and model names change often, check them against the current docs before you copy anything.
The map: a harness is a car
The video explains each part with a car. The model is the engine. Everything else is what makes it useful to drive.

items: Steering and GPS: the system prompt, plus streaming as the dashboard
Brakes and saved places: permissions and memory

blocks.text: Step 1: one call (the engine)

The first version sends one message and prints one reply. It teaches the three things every call needs: a model, a `max_tokens` limit, and a list of `messages`, each with a role of `user` or `assistant`. Nothing is remembered afterwards.
Step 2: the loop (the chassis)

To get a conversation, wrap the call in a loop. The key fact is that the model is stateless. It remembers nothing between calls. The harness keeps the whole history in a list and sends all of it every time.

blocks.code:
messages = []  # the entire conversation lives here

while True:
    user_input = input("you > ").strip()
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})

    response = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=MAX_TOKENS,
        messages=messages,
    )

    # Keep the full content (not just the text) so the history stays exact.
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

blocks.text: So the model's "memory" of the chat is really the harness resending the list. That also means every turn costs more than the last.
Step 3: tools and the agent loop (the wheels)
A tool has two halves. A schema tells the model the tool exists. A plain Python function does the work when the model asks.

The model never runs anything. It replies with a `tool_use` block that names a tool and its input. The harness runs the function and sends the result back as a `tool_result`. Repeat until the model stops asking.

This is the agent loop. One user message can now trigger many model calls. The demo gives the model five tools: list files, read a file, write a file, edit a file (replace one exact snippet that must match once) and run a shell command.
Step 4: system prompt and streaming (steering and the dashboard)
The system prompt tells the agent who it is and where it is working. Streaming prints tokens as they arrive, so you are not staring at a blank screen while a long answer is written.
Step 5: safety (the brakes) and memory (saved places)
Once an agent can write files and run commands, it needs limits. The demo adds four.
**Permission prompts.** Tools that change things are marked dangerous. The harness asks before running them.
**A workspace boundary.** File tools resolve every path and refuse anything outside the working folder.
**Timeouts and a turn limit.** Shell commands get a timeout, and `MAX_TURNS = 25` caps how many model calls one request may use, so a confused agent cannot loop forever.
**Memory.** A `MEMORY.md` file is loaded into the system prompt at startup, and a `remember` tool appends to it. That is how the agent knows something the next time you start it.
These checks live in the harness, not the model. A model can be asked to be careful, but only the harness can enforce it.
Step 6: context management (the fuel gauge)

Because the whole history is resent each turn, the context fills up. Step 6 tracks it. After every call the harness reads the token usage, and when the context passes a threshold it compacts: it asks the model to summarise the conversation, then replaces the history with that summary.

blocks.code:
COMPACT_AT = 150000  # compact once the context passes this many tokens

def compact(system, messages):
    request = messages + [{"role": "user", "content": COMPACT_PROMPT}]
    response = call_model(system, request, echo=False)
    summary = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")

    messages[:] = [
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Summary of our conversation so far:\n\n{summary}"},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "Got it. I'll continue from this summary."},
    ]

blocks.text: Slash commands finish the job: `/tokens` shows the context size, `/compact` summarises on demand, `/clear` starts over, `/save` stores the session, `/help` and `/exit` do what they say.
What to take away

items: The model is stateless. History, tools, limits and memory all live in the harness.
The agent loop is a few lines. What makes an agent good or bad is mostly what is wrapped around it.
Safety belongs in code you control: permissions, path checks, timeouts and turn limits.
Context is a budget. Track it and compact before it runs out.

blocks.text: To follow along, clone the repo and run `git checkout v1`, then `v2` and so on. `git diff v1 v2` shows exactly what each step adds. Watch the [full walkthrough on YouTube](https://youtu.be/AFkYlg4347c).
